html:
Coffee became the main export of El Salvador in the late 1800s and stayed so for a century. In 1881 and 1882 laws abolished the common lands of Indigenous and peasant villages to make way for coffee estates.

The volcanic slopes were ideal for coffee. As indigo lost value, the state sold off communal land, and a small group of families, often called the Fourteen Families, came to own much of the country's best land, banks and coffee mills. Peasants became seasonal pickers on land that had been theirs.

Coffee made El Salvador one of the richest states of Central America and one of the most unequal. The Great Depression crashed coffee prices and set the stage for the rising and massacre of 1932. Land hunger also drove migration into Honduras and later the civil war.
sum: Coffee became the main export of El Salvador in the late 1800s and stayed so for a century. In 1881 and 1882 laws abolished the common lands of Indigenous and peasant villages to make way for coffee estates.
